Its theological claim is that God's rescue of his people is not a marginal divine activity but the central event around which all of creation's response is organized.

Christological connection. Paul quotes v. 49 in Romans 15:9 as a description of Christ's mission among the nations. Jesus is the King who survived the ultimate enemy (death), whose rescue generated praise that has overflowed into every nation. The love of v. 1 — 'I love you, O LORD, my strength' — is the love of the Son for the Father who raised him, and the missionary impulse of v. 49 is the Great Commission.
18.examples:
Then: Psalm 18 was preserved in 2 Samuel 22 as a memorial of David's entire career — the retrospective testimony of a man who had been through everything and had found God faithful in all of it. The psalm was meant to be sung, remembered, rehearsed — kept alive in the community as a testimony to the kind of God Israel served.

Now: Every believer has their own Psalm 18 — the specific deliverance, the particular rescue, the moment when the cords of death were loosened and God reached down. The psalmist's discipline is to tell that story, to rehearse the 'wonderful deeds,' to say 'I love you, O LORD' not as a generic religious sentiment but as the specific response of a specific person to a specific act of God. These personal testimonies of deliverance, kept alive in community, are the living tradition that sustains faith in the next generation.

19.title: The Two Books: Creation and Torah
19.text: The heavens declare the glory of God, and the sky above proclaims his handiwork. Day to day pours out speech, and night to night reveals knowledge... The law of the LORD is perfect, reviving the soul; the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple... Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable in your sight, O LORD, my rock and my redeemer. (ESV)
19.overview:
Psalm 19 is widely regarded as the most beautiful psalm in the Psalter — a poem so perfectly constructed that C. S. Lewis called it 'the greatest poem in the Psalter and one of the greatest lyrics in the world.' It moves from the witness of creation (vv. 1–6) to the witness of Torah (vv. 7–11) to personal prayer (vv. 12–14) in a movement that is both literary and theological: the two great books of divine revelation (the book of nature and the book of Scripture) are read by the finite human creature who finds them simultaneously illuminating and convicting, and who ends in the only posture appropriate to such knowledge — humble petition for forgiveness and acceptance.

The theological claim of the psalm is that God has not left himself without witness. The heavens declare his glory — silently, continuously, to every person who has ever lived under the sky. And the Torah of the LORD illuminates what the heavens can only gesture toward: the character of the God who made them, the path of life he has prescribed, the warnings that protect the attentive soul, and the rewards that flow from covenant faithfulness. Paul's argument in Romans 1:19–20 and 2:14–15 is the theological unpacking of vv. 1–4; his argument in Romans 7 about the law's perfection and the soul's weakness is the unpacking of vv. 7–13.

The final verse — 'Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable in your sight, O LORD, my rock and my redeemer' — has become one of the most-used prayers in the church's history, used before sermons, before conversations, before any act of communication. It is the prayer of the creature who has seen how great God is and how great the gap between that greatness and human frailty, and who asks for the grace that alone can bridge it.

sections.title: The Silent Sermon of the Heavens
sections.commentary:
'The heavens declare the glory of God, and the sky above proclaims his handiwork.' The two verbs — declare (saphar) and proclaims (nagad) — are the same verbs used for deliberate verbal proclamation. The heavens are not merely backdrop; they are speakers, witnesses, preachers. Their testimony is to kavod — the glory, the overwhelming weightiness of God, his manifest significance and excellence. What the stars testify to is not beauty (though they are beautiful) but the character of the One who made them.

The paradox of vv. 2–4 is astonishing: 'There is no speech, nor are there words, whose voice is not heard.' The heavens speak without speech — their declaration is real but non-verbal, continuous but wordless. Paul unpacks this in Romans 10:18, quoting Psalm 19:4 to argue that the gospel has gone out to the whole world: 'Their voice has gone out to all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.' The natural revelation that preceded the gospel prepared humanity to receive it; the heavens' silent witness is the preface to the Word's speech.

The sun's daily circuit (vv. 4b–6) is treated with lyric expansiveness — a bridegroom coming from his chamber, a champion rejoicing to run his course. These are not the sun's own emotions; they are the poet's response to the testimony of the sun's faithful, joyful, powerful daily proclamation of the God who set it on its course. Every sunrise is a sermon about the God who governs the day. Every sunset is a testimony about the God who governs the night. The preacher who has stopped noticing this has become insensible to one of God's most persistent and universal communications.

sections.title: The Six Names of the Torah: Perfect, Sure, Right, Pure, Clean, True
sections.commentary:
The pivot from creation to Torah is dramatic and deliberate. The creation speaks of God's glory but cannot specify his character or his will; the Torah does both. In vv. 7–9, the Torah is described by six paired characteristics — each giving a name for the divine instruction and a description of what it does to the person who receives it. This is among the most concentrated and beautiful descriptions of Scripture in all of Scripture.

The law of the LORD is perfect, reviving the soul — tamim again, the word of wholeness and completeness. The Torah has no defect, no blind spot, no error. And it revives (meshib naphesh — restores the life of) the soul. It does not merely inform; it regenerates. The testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple — the Torah can be trusted absolutely, and it imparts wisdom to those who lack it naturally. The precepts of the LORD are right, rejoicing the heart — the commands of God are calibrated exactly for human flourishing; following them produces joy, not merely correctness. The commandment of the LORD is pure, enlightening the eyes — like the refined silver of Psalm 12, the commandment has no moral impurity; it is light for those groping in darkness. The fear of the LORD is clean, enduring forever — the reverence God's word produces is ceremonially and morally pure, and it is permanent. The rules of the LORD are true, and righteous altogether — every commandment corresponds exactly to reality as God has made it.

Verses 10–11: 'More to be desired are they than gold, even much fine gold; sweeter also than honey and drippings of the honeycomb. Moreover, by them is your servant warned; in keeping them there is great reward.' The Torah is simultaneously more valuable than any material treasure and more delightful than any sensory pleasure. The one who keeps it is warned of dangers invisible to natural perception and receives rewards that the unperceptive cannot see. This is not legalism — it is love for the word of the God who is loved.

sections.title: The Prayer of the Illuminated Creature
sections.commentary:
'Who can discern his errors? Declare me innocent from hidden faults.' The transition from the perfection of the Torah (v. 7) to the imperfection of the one who reads it (v. 12) is inevitable and honest. The clearer the standard, the more visible the gap. The person who has seen the Torah's perfection is simultaneously aware of their own imperfection — not just in the specific sins they can identify but in the 'hidden faults,' the errors too deep for self-perception. This is the Psalter's acknowledgment of what the New Testament will call the deceitfulness of sin (Heb. 3:13) and the unconscious self-deception of the fallen heart (Jer. 17:9).

'Keep back your servant also from presumptuous sins.' The contrast between hidden faults (v. 12) and presumptuous sins (v. 13) is the contrast between the sins of weakness and the sins of defiant rebellion — the sins with a high hand that the Torah treated as a different category from inadvertent sins (Num. 15:30). David is asking for two kinds of divine protection: illumination of what he cannot see, and restraint from what he can see and might choose anyway. Both are needed. Both require grace.

'Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable in your sight, O LORD, my rock and my redeemer.' The closing prayer unifies the two halves of the psalm: the words of my mouth (the spoken witness to the God of creation and Torah) and the meditation of my heart (the inner life shaped by the Torah's light) — both offered as a sacrifice to the God who is simultaneously the cosmic Rock and the personal Redeemer. Go'el — Redeemer — is the kinsman-redeemer, the one who buys back the family member from slavery or debt. The God of the heavens and the Torah is also the one who purchases back his people. That final name makes the entire psalm personal and salvific. The great witness of creation and Scripture ends not in information but in relationship.

19.theology:
Theme. Psalm 19 is the psalm of the two books — creation and Scripture — both of which witness to the one God whose glory fills the universe and whose law revives the soul. Its theological claim is that the God who reveals himself in the heavens has revealed himself more fully and personally in the Torah, and that the proper response to both revelations is the prayer of the humble creature who needs both warning and redemption.

Christological connection. Jesus Christ is the Word of God made flesh — the living Torah, the embodiment of the perfect, sure, right, pure, clean, and true instruction of God in a human life. He is the one who fulfilled every requirement of the Torah and bore the consequence of every violation, becoming the go'el — the Redeemer — who purchases back those whose hidden faults and presumptuous sins the Torah had exposed. In him, the two books of Psalm 19 are united: the Creator and the Redeemer are the same person.
19.examples:
Then: Israel's neighbors had creation myths in which the sun, moon, and stars were divine beings to be worshipped. Psalm 19's radical claim was that the heavens are not divine — they are witnesses to the divine. The sky does not speak for itself; it declares the glory of another. This demythologizing of nature was Israel's theological contribution to the ancient world, and it is the foundation of what would eventually become natural science: a universe that is not divine is a universe that can be investigated.

Now: The final verse of Psalm 19 has been used before sermons for two millennia because it names the preacher's deepest need: that the words of the mouth (what is spoken) and the meditation of the heart (what drives the speaking) would both be acceptable to God. This is not a formula but a theology of preaching — the recognition that proclamation of the God of creation and Scripture requires not just correct content but a heart aligned with the God it speaks about. Let the preacher pray it every time.

20.title: Prayer for the King Before Battle
20.text: May the LORD answer you in the day of trouble! May the name of the God of Jacob protect you! May he send you help from the sanctuary and give you support from Zion!... Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God. (ESV)
20.overview:
Psalm 20 is a royal intercession psalm — the congregation praying for the king before he goes to battle. It belongs to a pair with Psalm 21, which celebrates the answered prayer after victory. Together they frame the liturgical experience of Israel's holy war: prayer before, praise after, the God of Zion at the center of both. The psalm is not merely ancient military liturgy; it is a theological statement about the relationship between human action (the king going to war) and divine provision (the LORD answering from his holy heaven).

The theological center of the psalm is v. 7: 'Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God.' This is one of the great confessional contrasts of the Psalter — the two ultimate securities that every person and every nation must choose between. Chariots and horses represent the most sophisticated military technology of the ancient world; the name of the LORD represents the character and covenant commitment of the God of Israel. One is visible, measurable, and ultimately finite; the other is invisible, immeasurable, and eternal. The psalm does not forbid military preparation; it identifies where ultimate confidence must rest.

The Messianic dimension of the psalm is unmistakable: the king who is prayed for is the LORD's anointed (v. 6 — meshiach), and the confidence that God saves his anointed from his holy heaven points forward to the ultimate Anointed One whose salvation came not from the military success of chariots but from the power of God in resurrection. The congregation's intercession for the king is the template for the church's intercession for Christ's reign in the world.

sections.title: The Congregation's Prayer for the King
sections.commentary:
'May the LORD answer you in the day of trouble! May the name of the God of Jacob protect you!' The five-fold prayer of vv. 1–5 is structured by the repeated 'may' — a series of petitions, each one more specific, together forming a comprehensive intercession for the king who is about to lead Israel into battle. The 'day of trouble' is the day of battle — the moment of maximum vulnerability when the king's life and the nation's future hang in the balance. The congregation's first instinct is prayer, not strategy.

The specific petitions build: answer from the day of trouble (v. 1), protection from the name of God (v. 1), help from the sanctuary and support from Zion (v. 2), remembrance of the sacrifices offered (v. 3), fulfillment of all the king's plans (v. 4). The appeal to Zion and the sanctuary is important — the king does not go to war as an autonomous agent but as the representative of the God who dwells on the holy hill. The military campaign is embedded in the worship life of the nation.

'May he grant you your heart's desire and fulfill all your plans!' (v. 4). The prayer for the fulfillment of the king's plans is a prayer that the king's heart be aligned with God's purposes — because if it is, the fulfillment of his plans is the fulfillment of God's purposes. The prayer assumes, rather than demanding, that the king's heart is oriented toward God. It is the prayer of a congregation that trusts its king's integrity and prays that God will vindicate that trust through victory.

sections.title: Chariots or the Name: The Ultimate Contrast
sections.commentary:
'Now I know that the LORD saves his anointed; he will answer him from his holy heaven with the saving might of his right hand.' The sudden shift to 'now I know' — perhaps the voice of a priest or prophet interceding with a word of assurance — introduces the certainty that grounds the prayer of vv. 1–5. The king will be answered. The answer will come from the holy heaven — from the throne of God, not from earthly military calculation. The instrument of the answer is 'the saving might of his right hand' — the same right hand that brought Israel out of Egypt (Ps. 44:3; Ex. 15:6), the arm that has always been sufficient.

'Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God.' This is the confessional heart of the psalm and one of the most important verses in the Psalter. The antithesis is not between military preparation and prayer (Israel did maintain armies) but between ultimate confidence and contingent confidence. Chariots and horses are contingent — they can be defeated, destroyed, outmaneuvered. The name of the LORD is ultimate — it is the sum of his character, his covenant commitment, his irresistible power exercised on behalf of those who are his. Nations that trust ultimately in their military technology have a trust that can be shattered; nations that trust ultimately in the living God have a trust that cannot be.

The outcome: 'They collapse and fall, but we rise and stand upright' (v. 8). The armies that trusted in chariots are described as collapsing — the verb is graphic, a sudden stumbling and falling. The congregation that trusts in the name of the LORD rises and stands upright. The contrast in outcome corresponds exactly to the contrast in the object of trust. The military superiority of the enemy does not determine the outcome; the character of the God trusted by the people determines the outcome.

The closing prayer — 'O LORD, save the king! May he answer us when we call' (v. 9) — returns to the beginning. The king's salvation and the congregation's access to God are inseparable: a king saved by God becomes the mediating presence through whom the congregation itself has confidence in God's answer. This royal intercession points forward to the one King whose salvation opened the way for every member of his congregation to approach the throne with confidence (Heb. 4:16).

20.theology:
Theme. Psalm 20 is a royal intercession psalm structured by the contrast between trusting in military power and trusting in the name of the LORD. Its theological claim is that the ultimate security of God's people rests not in earthly instruments of power, however sophisticated, but in the character and covenant commitment of the God who answers from his holy heaven.

Christological connection. The king who is prayed for — the LORD's anointed (meshiach) — finds his ultimate fulfillment in Jesus Christ. The congregation prays for the king's plans to be fulfilled; the Father's answer to the ultimate King was the resurrection, the vindication of his plans, the fulfillment of everything the anointed one set out to accomplish. The church's ongoing intercession — 'Your kingdom come, your will be done' — is the New Testament continuation of Psalm 20's pre-battle prayer.
20.examples:
Then: Israel's repeated temptation was to trust in alliances with Egypt (whose military superiority lay precisely in chariots and horses — Ex. 14:23; Isa. 31:1–3) rather than in the name of the LORD. Psalm 20 was the liturgical counter-formation: every time the king went to battle, the congregation proclaimed that ultimate confidence was in the name, not the horses. Isaiah 31:1 makes the same point directly: 'Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help and rely on horses.'

Now: The contemporary equivalents of 'chariots and horses' are the various sources of security that culture offers as alternatives to trust in God: financial reserves, political power, institutional strength, technological advantage, personal reputation. None of these are inherently wrong, but none of them can bear the weight of ultimate trust. Psalm 20 calls the church to the same confession that Israel made before every battle: we trust in the name of the LORD our God. That name is the only security that does not collapse.

21.title: Thanksgiving for the King's Victory
21.text: O LORD, in your strength the king rejoices, and in your salvation how greatly he exults! You have given him his heart's desire and have not withheld the request of his lips.... For the king trusts in the LORD, and through the steadfast love of the Most High he shall not be moved.... Be exalted, O LORD, in your strength! We will sing and praise your power. (ESV)
21.overview:
Psalm 21 is the answer to Psalm 20. Where Psalm 20 was the congregation's prayer for the king before the battle — 'May the LORD answer you in the day of trouble' — Psalm 21 is their praise after the victory: 'You have given him his heart's desire.' The prayer has been heard. The pair belongs together, and together they frame the whole rhythm of the life of faith: we ask before, we give thanks after, and the God of Zion stands at the centre of both.

The striking thing about the psalm is where it puts the credit. A king returning from war might be expected to celebrate his own courage and skill. This king does the opposite. Every verb points away from him and toward God: 'in your strength,' 'in your salvation,' 'you have given,' 'you meet him,' 'you set a crown.' The victory is real, but it is received, not achieved. And at the heart of the psalm (v. 7) stands the same confession that anchored Psalm 20: not 'the king is mighty' but 'the king trusts in the LORD.' That trust, and God's steadfast love answering it, is the true engine of everything the psalm celebrates.

And the psalm strains beyond any earthly king. He 'asked life' and was given 'length of days forever and ever' (v. 4); he is 'crowned' with gold (v. 3) and made 'glad with the joy of your presence' (v. 6). No son of David who ever sat on a throne in Jerusalem received that in full. It waited for great David's greater Son — the anointed King who trusted his Father to the cross, was given life that death could not hold, and now wears the crown 'of glory and honour' forever (Heb. 2:9). Read on the far side of the resurrection, Psalm 21 is a song about Christ the risen King, and about the joy of everyone who belongs to him.

sections.title: The Blessings God Gives the King
sections.commentary:
'O LORD, in your strength the king rejoices, and in your salvation how greatly he exults!' The psalm opens on a note of overflowing joy — and notice at once whose strength and whose salvation. The king is not glad in his army or his own arm; he is glad in the LORD. Joy that rests on what God has done is the only joy that cannot be taken away when circumstances change.

The blessings then tumble out, one after another, and each is plainly a gift: God 'gave him his heart's desire' and did not withhold 'the request of his lips' (v. 2) — the very prayers of Psalm 20 now answered; God 'meets him with rich blessings' and sets 'a crown of fine gold upon his head' (v. 3) — the crown is placed there by God, not seized by the king; God gave him 'life... length of days forever and ever' (v. 4); God bestows 'splendour and majesty' (v. 5). The king contributes nothing but the asking. God supplies everything else.

'Length of days forever and ever' (v. 4) is more than a courtly wish for a long reign. The words overflow the cup they are poured into. No mortal king lives forever; the phrase reaches past David to the King who would ask life of his Father in Gethsemane and receive it back in resurrection, 'the days of days' that never end (cf. Ps. 16:10–11; Heb. 7:16, 'the power of an indestructible life'). The Spirit tucks the eternal into the language of the temporal, and the New Testament unfolds it.

But the crown of the passage is v. 6: God makes him 'glad with the joy of your presence.' Deeper than the crown, deeper than the victory, deeper than the long life, is this — the gladness of being with God. The greatest gift God gives is never merely his gifts; it is himself. That is the joy the king prizes most, and it is the joy held out to every believer, whose true and lasting reward is 'fullness of joy' in God's own presence (Ps. 16:11).

sections.title: The Heart of It: The King Trusts in the LORD
sections.commentary:
'For the king trusts in the LORD, and through the steadfast love of the Most High he shall not be moved.' Here is the hinge of the whole psalm, and it is a deliberate echo of the confession at the centre of Psalm 20 — 'some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God' (20:7). The victory just celebrated did not spring from the king's greatness. It sprang from his trust, and from the covenant love that met that trust.

Two words carry the verse. 'Trusts' names what the king did — he leaned his whole weight on God rather than on himself. 'Steadfast love' (Hebrew chesed — God's loyal, covenant-keeping love) names what God is, the faithfulness that will not let go of the one who leans on it. Put them together and you get the result: 'he shall not be moved.' Not because the king is strong, but because the One he trusts is.

This is the quiet secret of every settled life. The person who trusts in his own strength is only ever as secure as his strength — which is to say, not secure at all, for it fails. The person who trusts in the steadfast love of the Most High rests on something that cannot fail, and so cannot finally be shaken (cf. Ps. 125:1: 'those who trust in the LORD are like Mount Zion, which cannot be moved'). What was true of the king is true of the least believer who takes the same refuge.

sections.title: The Triumph Over Enemies and the LORD Exalted
sections.commentary:
The psalm now turns to the certain defeat of the king's enemies (vv. 8–12), and the imagery is fierce: God's hand will 'find out' all who hate him; they will become 'a blazing oven,' swallowed up in wrath, consumed by fire (v. 9); their plots, however cleverly devised, 'will not succeed' (v. 11). Modern readers often flinch here, so two things must be said plainly. First, this is not a licence for the king's personal vengeance — the acting hand throughout is God's: 'the LORD will swallow them up.' Judgment belongs to him, not to us (Rom. 12:19). Second, this is the sober truth the whole Bible tells: God is real, evil is real, and God will not let evil stand forever. The same fire that terrifies the rebel is the safety of the oppressed, who need to know that wickedness does not get the last word.

Read forward, these verses describe the final triumph of Christ the King over every power that sets itself against him (cf. Ps. 2; 1 Cor. 15:25, 'he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet'; 2 Thess. 1:7–9). The astonishing mercy of the gospel is that the King who will one day judge his enemies first came to make peace with them at the cost of his own blood — so that rebels might lay down their arms and become sons before that day arrives.

And then the last word (v. 13): 'Be exalted, O LORD, in your strength! We will sing and praise your power.' Notice who is lifted high at the end. Not the king — the LORD. The whole psalm has been building to this: every blessing traced back to God, every victory credited to God, and now the congregation turns the celebration into worship. That is the goal of every good gift and every answered prayer — that God would be exalted and his people would sing. It is where Psalm 20's prayer and Psalm 21's praise were always heading.

21.theology:
Theme. Psalm 21 is a royal thanksgiving — the celebration of a victory received as pure gift from God. Its structure moves from the blessings God gives the king (vv. 1–6), to the trust at the heart of it all (v. 7), to the certain overthrow of God's enemies and the exaltation of the LORD (vv. 8–13). Its governing conviction is that God is the source of every good the king enjoys, and God is the one to whom all the glory returns.

Grace, not achievement. The relentless second-person verbs ('you gave,' 'you meet,' 'you set,' 'you bestow,' 'you make') teach a theology of grace: the king's crown, life, glory, and joy are all conferred, not earned. This is the Old Testament in miniature of what Paul will say plainly — 'what do you have that you did not receive?' (1 Cor. 4:7).

Trust and steadfast love. Verse 7 ties the king's security to two things: his trust and God's chesed (covenant love). Human faith and divine faithfulness meet, and the result is a life that 'shall not be moved.' The security of the believer rests not on the strength of his faith but on the object of it — the unchanging love of the Most High.

Messianic and eschatological. The gift of 'life... forever and ever' (v. 4), the crown, and the joy of God's presence reach past every mortal king to the risen Christ, the anointed King who lives forever and reigns until every enemy is subdued (1 Cor. 15:25). The fiery judgment of vv. 8–12 is God's, not man's, and finds its resolution in the return of Christ, when he is 'glorified in his saints' and his enemies face his justice (2 Thess. 1:7–10).
21.examples:
Then: When Israel's king came home from war, this psalm put words in the congregation's mouth that refused to flatter him. They did not sing 'how great is the king'; they sang 'in your strength, O LORD, the king rejoices.' It was a deliberate discipline of memory — training a whole nation to trace victory back to God rather than to the man on the throne, the same lesson Psalm 20 taught before the battle. Every celebration became an act of worship rather than an act of hero-making.

Now: Old Joe needs this psalm the day after something goes right — the promotion, the recovery, the answered prayer, the crisis survived. The human heart's instinct at the top of the hill is to say 'I did it,' or to let the joy rest on the achievement itself. Psalm 21 retrains the instinct: every good thing is a gift received from an open-handed God (Jas. 1:17), and the deepest joy is not the gift but the Giver — 'the joy of your presence' (v. 6). Credit God out loud. Rest your security not in your own strength, which fails, but in the steadfast love of the Most High, which does not (v. 7). And when you have been given much, let the celebration turn, as this one does, into song: 'Be exalted, O LORD.' Above all, let the psalm lift your eyes to the King it finally sings about — Christ, who trusted his Father, was crowned through the cross, was given life forever, and now shares his own joy and his unshakeable security with everyone who trusts in him.

22.title: The Psalm of the Cross: Forsaken, Then Praised to the Ends of the Earth
22.text: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Why are you so far from saving me, from the words of my groaning?... they have pierced my hands and feet — I can count all my bones — they stare and gloat over me; they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots.... Posterity shall serve him; it shall be told of the Lord to the coming generation; they shall come and proclaim his righteousness to a people yet unborn, that he has done it. (ESV)
22.overview:
Psalm 22 is the psalm of the cross. No other passage in the Old Testament is quoted more often in the accounts of Jesus' crucifixion, and its opening line was on his own lips as he died: 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?' (Matt. 27:46). It begins in the deepest darkness a soul can know — the sense of being abandoned by God — and travels all the way to the ends of the earth bowing down in worship. It is, in one psalm, Good Friday and Easter and the mission to the nations.

David wrote it out of some agony of his own; we are not told which. But the details reach far past anything David ever suffered. A man surrounded by enemies who 'pierce my hands and feet' (v. 16), whose bones are pulled out of joint and who is 'poured out like water' (v. 14), whose garments are gambled for (v. 18) — and all of this written roughly a thousand years before the Romans made crucifixion their instrument of death. The Spirit gave David words whose full weight only one Man would ever carry. This is prophecy not merely in a prediction here and there, but in the whole shape of the psalm: the righteous sufferer, forsaken and vindicated.

The turn comes at v. 22. Suddenly the lament becomes praise: 'I will tell of your name to my brothers.' Hebrews 2:12 puts that very verse in the mouth of the risen Christ, standing among the people his death has saved and calling them his brothers. From there the psalm opens outward like a flood — the afflicted eat and are satisfied (v. 26), 'all the ends of the earth' remember and turn to the LORD (v. 27), and the last word is a finished work handed on to 'a people yet unborn' — 'he has done it' (v. 31), an Old Testament whisper of 'It is finished' (John 19:30).

sections.title: The Cry: My God, Why Have You Forsaken Me?
sections.commentary:
'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?' There is no darker sentence in the Psalter, and no more important one to read slowly. It is a real cry of abandonment — not play-acting, not exaggeration. Yet notice what it is not: it is not the cry of an atheist or a man who has let go of God. Twice he says 'my God.' Even forsaken, he will not stop holding on. This is faith crying out in the dark — the hardest and highest kind of faith, which keeps addressing God even when God seems to have withdrawn.

When Jesus prayed this line from the cross, he was not merely borrowing a fitting quotation. He was entering the reality the words describe. In that hour the sinless Son bore the sin of his people, and the fellowship with his Father that he had known from all eternity was, for our sake, eclipsed. Why was he forsaken? So that we never would be. He took the abandonment our sin deserved so that to us God could say, 'I will never leave you nor forsake you' (Heb. 13:5). The blackest verse in the Psalms is the ground of the believer's deepest comfort.

The sufferer reaches for two anchors in the dark. First, God's character: 'Yet you are holy, enthroned on the praises of Israel' (v. 3) — God has not changed, however things feel. Second, God's track record: 'In you our fathers trusted; they trusted, and you delivered them' (vv. 4–5). When feelings testify that God has gone, memory and Scripture testify that he is faithful. Then the humiliation deepens — 'I am a worm and not a man, scorned by mankind' (v. 6) — and the mockers sneer the cruellest taunt of all: 'He trusts in the LORD; let him deliver him' (v. 8). Matthew records the chief priests throwing those very words at the crucified Christ (Matt. 27:43). The psalm was being fulfilled to the syllable while they spoke.

sections.title: The Suffering: Poured Out Like Water, Hands and Feet Pierced
sections.commentary:
Verses 12–18 take us inside the suffering, and the language turns almost unbearably physical. Enemies close in like 'strong bulls of Bashan' (v. 12) and 'a roaring lion' (v. 13). Then the body itself gives way: 'I am poured out like water, and all my bones are out of joint' (v. 14) — exactly what happens to a body hung by its arms; 'my heart is like wax, melted within my breast'; 'my strength is dried up... my tongue sticks to my jaws' (v. 15) — the raging thirst of the dying, and behind the Gospel word 'I thirst' (John 19:28).

Then the astonishing line: 'they have pierced my hands and feet' (v. 16). A brief honest note, because a careful reader with a study Bible will meet it: the traditional Hebrew here is difficult, and one reading is 'like a lion my hands and feet.' But the ancient Greek translation (made before Christ), the oldest manuscripts among the Dead Sea Scrolls, and the earliest versions all support 'pierced.' It is not a Christian alteration; it is the older, better-attested reading — and it describes, a millennium in advance, the one form of execution that pierces exactly the hands and the feet. 'I can count all my bones' (v. 17) fits the same scene: a body stretched and exposed, stared at by a gloating crowd.

And then the detail no imagination would invent: 'they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots' (v. 18). John records the soldiers at the foot of the cross doing precisely this — tearing the outer clothes into shares but rolling dice for the seamless tunic rather than ruin it — and quotes this verse as fulfilled before their eyes (John 19:23–24). They did not know they were reading their lines from a thousand-year-old script. The section ends where such suffering can only end, in prayer: 'But you, O LORD, do not be far off!' (v. 19).

sections.title: The Turn: From Forsaken to the Praise of the Nations
sections.commentary:
At verse 22 the psalm breaks — the way a fever breaks. The darkness does not gradually lighten; it turns, all at once, into praise: 'I will tell of your name to my brothers; in the midst of the congregation I will praise you.' The cry of the forsaken has become the song of the delivered. What lies between v. 21 and v. 22, unwritten, is rescue. For David, some deliverance from his trouble; for the greater Sufferer, nothing less than resurrection. Hebrews 2:12 quotes this verse as the word of the risen Christ, who is not ashamed to stand among the people his death has purchased and call them 'brothers.' The forsaken one is now surrounded by a family.

From there the circle of praise widens until it takes in the whole world. First the 'great congregation' of Israel (v. 25); then 'the afflicted shall eat and be satisfied' (v. 26) — the hungry fed at the table the Sufferer's victory has spread; then, breaking every boundary, 'all the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the LORD, and all the families of the nations shall worship before you' (v. 27). The suffering of one Man becomes the salvation of the nations. Even 'those who go down to the dust' and generations 'yet unborn' are swept in (vv. 29–31) — this gospel is for the dying and for the not-yet-born, which is to say, for us.

And the final phrase seals it: 'they shall come and proclaim his righteousness to a people yet unborn, that he has done it' (v. 31). It is finished. The work is complete, accomplished by the Sufferer alone, and all that remains for the coming generations is to receive it and pass it on. A thousand years before Calvary, the psalm that began with the cry of dereliction ends on the note of a finished salvation — the same note the dying Christ would sound in three words: 'It is finished' (John 19:30).

22.theology:
Theme. Psalm 22 moves in two great movements: the suffering of the righteous one (vv. 1–21) and the praise that follows his vindication (vv. 22–31). It is the fullest Old Testament portrait of substitutionary suffering leading to worldwide salvation — lament that turns to global praise because the sufferer is delivered.

The forsakenness of the cross. Verse 1, spoken by Jesus, opens the deepest mystery of the atonement: the Son bearing sin experiences the eclipse of the Father's felt presence, the judgment due to sinners falling on the sinless substitute (2 Cor. 5:21). This is not the Trinity divided — the Son never ceased to be beloved — but the Son, as sin-bearer, drinking the cup of wrath so that his people are spared it. He was forsaken that we might be received.

Prophecy and providence. The specific correspondences — pierced hands and feet, garments gambled for, mockery in the very words used at Golgotha, consuming thirst — display a detailed prophetic witness written a thousand years before crucifixion existed. This is not David decoding the future but the Spirit shaping David's genuine suffering into a template that only Christ would fill completely (cf. 1 Pet. 1:10–11).

Resurrection and mission. The turn at v. 22 (applied to the risen Christ in Heb. 2:12) grounds the church's very existence: the delivered Sufferer gathers 'brothers,' and the worship spreads to 'all the ends of the earth' (v. 27). The finished work — 'he has done it' (v. 31) — is the engine of world mission: a completed salvation to be proclaimed, not a project to be finished.
22.examples:
Then: For Israel, Psalm 22 gave language to the darkest experience of faith — the sense that God had withdrawn — without letting go of God. The worshipper in agony could pray these very words and still say 'my God,' anchoring himself to God's holiness and God's past faithfulness when his own feelings testified otherwise. It taught a suffering people to lament toward God rather than away from him.

Now: Old Joe will one day walk through a valley where God feels absent — a grief, an illness, a long unanswered prayer — and Psalm 22 hands him two gifts. First, permission: the most faithful thing you can do in the dark is to cry out to God, honestly, as Jesus himself did; the question 'why?' flung toward heaven is not unbelief but faith refusing to stop talking to God. Second, and deeper, the certainty that he will never actually be forsaken — because Jesus already was, in his place. When you feel abandoned, look to the One who truly was abandoned so that you never will be. And notice where the psalm goes: the darkness is not the end of the story. It breaks into praise, and the praise runs out to the ends of the earth. The cross you cling to in the dark is the same cross that is saving the nations and reaching, across a thousand generations, all the way to you — because 'he has done it.'

23.title: The LORD Is My Shepherd
23.text: The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters.... Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me; your rod and your staff, they comfort me.... Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life, and I shall dwell in the house of the LORD forever. (ESV)
23.overview:
Psalm 23 is the most loved of all the psalms, and for good reason: in six short verses it says what the whole Bible says about God's care for his people. It has been whispered at deathbeds, prayed in prisons, sung at gravesides, and clung to in ten thousand ordinary fears. David, who had been a shepherd before he was a king, looks back at how he once cared for helpless sheep and says, in effect: that is what the LORD is to me.

The psalm turns on two pictures. In the first (vv. 1–4), God is the Shepherd who provides, restores, guides, and walks with his sheep even through the darkest valley. In the second (vv. 5–6), God becomes the Host who spreads a table, anoints the head, fills the cup, and welcomes the guest into his house forever. Both pictures say the same thing from two angles: the believer is completely, personally, tenderly cared for by God himself.

And the New Testament hands us the key that unlocks it. 'I am the good shepherd,' said Jesus. 'The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep' (John 10:11). Psalm 23 is not merely a lovely poem about God in general; it is a portrait of Christ, the Shepherd who went down into the valley of the shadow of death himself — and came out the other side — so that his sheep could follow him through it without fear.

sections.title: The Shepherd: Provision, Rest, and Restoration
sections.commentary:
'The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.' Everything is in that first line. Not 'the LORD is a shepherd' but 'my shepherd' — the God who flung the stars into space stoops to care for one small life by name. And a sheep is not a flattering thing to be compared to: sheep are defenceless, prone to wander, unable to find food or water or their way home on their own. That is the honest picture of us. But the point of the verse is not the weakness of the sheep; it is the sufficiency of the Shepherd. Because this Shepherd is mine, 'I shall not want' — I will lack nothing I truly need.

'He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters' (v. 2). Anyone who has kept sheep knows they will not lie down while they are hungry, frightened, or unsettled — so rest itself is evidence that the Shepherd has met every need. The 'still waters' are, literally, waters of rest; sheep are afraid of fast-moving streams, so the shepherd finds them quiet pools they can drink from without fear. God does not drive his people; he leads them to rest.

'He restores my soul. He leads me in paths of righteousness for his name's sake' (v. 3). To 'restore the soul' is the shepherd's work of bringing back the sheep that has wandered off or collapsed exhausted — reviving it, setting it on its feet, returning it to the flock. And he leads in 'right paths' — the good and safe ways — and here is a phrase not to hurry past: 'for his name's sake.' The Shepherd guides us rightly not only for our good but for his own reputation. His honour is bound up with getting his sheep home. That is why our final safety does not finally rest on our poor sense of direction, but on his name.

sections.title: Through the Valley: 'You Are With Me'
sections.commentary:
'Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me' (v. 4). This is the heart of the psalm, and something quiet and profound happens right here. Up to now David has spoken about God — 'he makes me,' 'he leads me.' But the moment he enters the valley, he turns and speaks to God: 'for you are with me.' In the darkest place, the relationship becomes most personal. The valley does not push God away; it draws the sheep closer to the Shepherd's side.

The phrase 'valley of the shadow of death' names the deepest darkness a life can pass through — and yes, death itself, but not only death: any place of danger, grief, or dread where the light seems to fail. Notice what David does not say. He does not say the valley is removed, or that the sheep is carried around it. He says 'I walk through' — there is a way in and, thank God, a way out — and that he will 'fear no evil.' Why? Not because the valley is not dark, but because he is not alone in it: 'you are with me.' The cure for fear is not the absence of danger but the presence of the Shepherd.

'Your rod and your staff, they comfort me.' Two tools, two comforts. The rod was a stout club the shepherd carried to beat off wolves and lions — it speaks of protection, the Shepherd fighting for the sheep. The staff was the long crook used to guide the flock and to hook a fallen sheep and lift it back to safety — it speaks of gentle rescue. Strength to defend and tenderness to rescue: both are in the Shepherd's hand, and both are a comfort in the dark.

sections.title: The Host: The Table, the Overflowing Cup, and the House Forever
sections.commentary:
At verse 5 the picture changes. The Shepherd becomes a Host: 'You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies.' This is astonishing calm. God does not wait until the enemies are gone to bless his guest; he spreads a feast right in front of them, and the guest sits and eats in peace while they look on, unable to touch him. The believer's security is so complete that he can feast in the middle of a battlefield.

'You anoint my head with oil; my cup overflows.' To pour oil on a guest's head was the mark of honour and glad welcome — you were treated not as a bare necessity but as a delight. And the cup is not merely filled; it overflows. God's care is never grudging or exact; it spills over. He gives more than enough.

'Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life' (v. 6). The word behind 'follow' is stronger than it sounds in English — it means to pursue, to chase after, the same word used elsewhere for enemies hunting a man down. Here it is turned inside out into pure grace: what pursues the believer, all his days, is not disaster but God's own goodness and steadfast love, hunting him down to bless him. And the last line lifts the whole psalm into eternity: 'I shall dwell in the house of the LORD forever.' The sheep that is provided for, restored, walked through the valley, and feasted is finally brought home — into God's own house, to stay. That is where the Good Shepherd, who laid down his life for the sheep, is leading every one of his flock (John 10:11; 14:2–3).

23.theology:
Theme. Psalm 23 is a psalm of confident trust, built on two images of God's total care — the Shepherd (vv. 1–4) and the Host (vv. 5–6). Its logic is not that the believer's life is free of danger (there are enemies and a death-dark valley) but that in every circumstance the believer is personally, sufficiently cared for by God.

Providence and preservation. Provision ('I shall not want'), rest, restoration, and right guidance are all the Shepherd's doing, grounded finally in his own name and honour (v. 3). The perseverance of the believer rests not on the sheep's competence but on the Shepherd's commitment — a commitment bound up with his reputation, and therefore certain.

God with us in death. Verse 4 is one of the Bible's great comforts in dying: the valley is real and must be walked through, but the Shepherd walks it too. The shift from 'he' to 'you' shows that suffering, far from proving God absent, is where his presence is most keenly known.

Christ the Good Shepherd. Jesus claims this psalm as his own (John 10:11), and fills it: he is the Shepherd who provides and guides, who himself passed through the valley of death and rose, and who leads his flock to the Father's house (John 14:2–3). The overflowing cup and the table before enemies find their echo in the Lord's Supper and their consummation in the marriage supper of the Lamb (Rev. 19:9).
23.examples:
Then: For Israel — and for the shepherd-king who wrote it — this psalm turned the everyday realities of pasture, water, predators, and the shepherd's crook into a confession of trust. It gave a people who lived close to danger a way to say that their real security was not their circumstances but their God, who led them like a flock (cf. Ps. 80:1).

Now: Old Joe reaches for Psalm 23 in exactly the places it was made for — the hospital waiting-room, the sleepless night, the open grave, the season when enemies or fears press in. Its comfort is not that the valley will be avoided but that he will not walk it alone: 'you are with me.' When he cannot see the way, the Shepherd's honour is staked on getting him home ('for his name's sake'). When he is hunted by worry, he is reminded that what is really pursuing him, all his days, is God's goodness and mercy. And when he fears death itself, he looks to the Good Shepherd who walked through that valley first and came out alive — and who has promised that the last stop for every sheep is not the grave but the Father's house, forever. Let this psalm be learned by heart while the sun shines; it is the best of company in the dark.
